title: Long-lived divergence from equilibrium of electrons, nuclear spins and lattice for a solid state ion trap at low temperature
authors: Guy Matmon, Manuel Grimm, Markus Mueller, Byron J. Villis, Andrew J. Fisher, Gabriel Aeppli
abstract: A fundamental problem in physics as well as engineering is equilibration. For example, the regulation of thermal and quantum fluctuations enables thermal and quantum annealing of complex systems. A key question is how different subsystems, such as electrons, nuclear spins and phonons equilibrate on their own as well as with each other. Level crossings play a special role in the dynamics of coupled degrees of freedom, for it is here that entanglement can be maximized to speed up relaxation. Here we use optical methods to establish the electronuclear level scheme, including avoided and unavoided crossings, and to examine equilibration of a rare earth ion (Ho$^{3+}$) in a salt (LiYF$_4$), a model system with quantum fluctuations which can be tuned via an external magnetic field transverse to the crystallographic long axis of the tetragonal host. We track the state of the system by monitoring the populations of the levels as a function of swept longitudinal fields, and discover that at low temperatures, depending on the experimental protocol, vastly different non-equilibrium states arise. We find evidence that nuclear spin excitations diffuse and equilibrate without the assistance of phonons, and tend to acquire higher effective temperatures than the electronic spins and the yet cooler lattice. A theory of thermally assisted tunneling rules out the standard scenario of phonon -assisted tunneling, and instead suggests that fast dynamics at level anti-crossings are facilitated entirely by nuclear spin diffusion. This provides a new understanding of thermalization and related slow relaxation phenomena in dense, multi-component interacting quantum systems.
summary: This research explores the complex issue of thermalization in a solid-state ion trap system by studying the coupling between electron, nuclear spin, and lattice degrees of freedom. Using optical spectroscopy and magnetization measurements, the authors demonstrate that at very low temperatures, the system can maintain distinct, non-equilibrium temperatures for its various components. This suggests that energy dissipation pathways are highly dependent on the experimental history and that nuclear spin dynamics play a crucial, non-phonon-mediated role in relaxation.
main_problem: The paper investigates the fundamental problem of equilibration, specifically how different quantum subsystems (electrons, nuclear spins, and lattice/phonons) thermalize among themselves and with each other at low temperatures.
main_result: The authors find evidence that at low temperatures, the system can enter vastly different non-equilibrium states depending on the experimental protocol, with nuclear spins showing signs of diffusing and equilibrating independently of the lattice.
method: The study combines high-resolution optical spectroscopy (FTIR) and magnetization measurements (Faraday rotation) with theoretical modeling to track state populations and energy levels.
model_or_system: The system is a solid-state ion trap using a rare earth ion ($	ext{Ho}^{3+}$) in a salt ($	ext{LiYF}_4$), which acts as a model for coupled electron-nuclear spin dynamics in a solid matrix.
key_observables: Population of the 16 hyperfine states, effective electronic and nuclear spin temperatures ($T_e, T_n$), and magnetization hysteresis loops.
important_parameters: Low temperatures (sub-Kelvin regime), external magnetic fields ($B_z, B_x$), and the coupling strengths between spin and lattice degrees of freedom.
main_assumptions: The standard scenario of phonon-assisted tunneling is ruled out by theory, and the analysis relies on fitting state populations to Gibbs distributions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the mapping of electronuclear level schemes via avoided crossings, the divergence of measured spin temperatures ($T_e, T_n$) from the lattice temperature ($T_{sample}$), and the closing of temperature hysteresis with increasing transverse fields.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the general problem of equilibration to detailing the experimental measurements on the $	ext{Ho}^{3+}$ system, presenting evidence for non-equilibrium temperature distributions, and finally proposing theoretical insights into the dominant relaxation mechanisms (e.g., nuclear spin diffusion facilitating fast dynamics).
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it tackles non-equilibrium dynamics in strongly coupled quantum systems, providing experimental evidence for energy partitioning and relaxation pathways that deviate significantly from simple thermal models, which is crucial for quantum control.
